title: Shattered Glass
full_review:
����������� A hotshot journalist becomes entangled in the web of his own deceits in director Billy Ray's fact-based drama "Shattered Glass" (Lions Gate).

The middling biopic chronicles the self-imploding career of Stephen Glass (Hayden Christensen), a staff writer for the influential public-policy journal, The New Republic, whose rising-star status had, by the mid-1990s, made him one of the most sought-after, young-gun stringers in Washington.

Respected by his peers and beloved by his co-workers, Glass is depicted as a hyper-talented upstart, both cocksure and humbled by the responsibility of writing for a publication self-billed as "the in-flight magazine of Air Force One." Yet from the opening sequence Glass shows signs of shattering, exhibiting bipolar waves of self-assuredness and nerdy insecurity.

Glass' fast track to Pulitzerville hits a major speed bump when a Forbes online reporter, Adam Penenberg (Steve Zahn), confronts Charles Lane (Peter Sarsgaard), then editor of The New Republic, with charges that Glass totally fabricated a story concerning a young computer hacker's sweetheart deal with a nonexistent dot-com firm.

Faced with an ethical time bomb that could jeopardize the reputation of the respected magazine, Lane confronts Glass, who, sticking to his guns, denies any wrongdoing. An internecine battle ensues with most of the writing staff, which views Lane's ethical crusade as a smokescreen to oust the more popular Glass, sympathizing with the shamed wonder boy. The remainder of the film becomes a mental game of cat and mouse as Lane begins to systematically check the veracity not only of the article in question, but of all Glass' previous writings, uncovering a pattern of fraud and deception.

While examining issues of public trust and the role of the press in a free society, the film lacks the sense of cultural importance achieved by "All the President's Men" -- the 1976 film about the heroic reporters who blew the lid off the Watergate scandal -- though it does strike a timely chord given the recent controversy surrounding Jayson Blair and The New York Times.

Based on Buzz Bissinger's Vanity Fair expose on Glass, the film, though full of lofty ideals, ultimately proves an emotionally unsatisfying defense of journalistic integrity.

Christensen, whose insipid performance as a young Darth Vader gives new meaning to the phrase "working stiff," seems lost in the complex role, weighing down an otherwise strong ensemble cast (including Hank Azaria and Chloe Sevigny). Far from an intrepid Gen-X Woodward or Bernstein, who could bamboozle editors seemingly at will, Christensen's Glass is a study in adenoidal blandness, as much a chronic whiner as he is a compulsive liar.

In the opening voiceover, Glass explains that journalism is about capturing behavior in order to understand why people act the way they do -- a question left glaringly unanswered during the ensuing 103 minutes. While the film plays like a modern Greek tragedy, it offers scant insight -- beyond some cursory remarks about Glass' hard-to-please parents -- into what prompted its flawed protagonist to indulge in such irrational and unconscionable dishonesty.

At one point the film's antihero concludes that people don't want to be informed but entertained. Regrettably, on both counts, this "Shattered Glass" is only half-full.

Due to some rough and sexually crude language and sporadic profanity, as well as an instance of drug abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
